title: My daughter-in-law told everyone I was too poor to attend her $90,000 wedding. Then the venue owner recognized my name and said, 'Ma'am, this entire estate belongs to you.' (PART 2)

blocks.text: The property manager, Mr. Gaines, had managed the estate for my father's trust for thirty years. My father, a tobacco farmer who'd struck it lucky when a highway was built through his land, bought the mountain property in 1968 and placed it in a trust "for my daughter, when she needs it." He died in 1983, when I was thirty-three and recently divorced. Something went wrong with the trust's paperwork, and his lawyer died a year later. The trustees, a bank in Charlotte, kept managing the estate, renting it out for weddings and retreats, waiting for a claim that never came. I'd never known it existed. My father had told me only that he'd "put something away for me in the hills."
Madison's father, Richard Harmon, was a developer. Two years earlier, he'd tried to buy the estate.

The bank refused because the trust's beneficiary had never been located and couldn't sign. Richard hired investigators. They traced the trust to me, and then to my son. Richard couldn't buy the estate from me directly, because he knew I'd ask questions. So his daughter introduced herself to Christopher at a gym. Eighteen months later, they were engaged.

The plan, according to emails Mr. Gaines had obtained from the bank, was for Madison to marry Christopher, help him "manage his aging mother's affairs," and eventually persuade me to sign a power of attorney and sell the estate to her father's company for a fraction of its value.
They'd chosen my estate for the wedding so Richard could show it to investors. And they'd kept me away so I'd never meet Mr. Gaines.
I walked into the bridal suite with the emails in my hand.
Christopher was there, in his tuxedo. I asked him to read them. He read the first page, then the second. Then he took off his boutonniere and set it on the table.
There was no wedding that day. The guests ate the food anyway, which I paid for, since it was my estate.
Christopher moved back in with me for a few months. He kept apologizing for not defending me. I told him he'd defended me when it mattered.

The trust's paperwork was corrected. The estate is mine now. I don't live there. It's still a wedding venue, but now a portion of every booking goes to a scholarship fund for children of farmworkers in my father's name.
Last summer, Christopher brought a new girlfriend to meet me. A schoolteacher. The first thing she asked was whether I'd like to come to dinner. No folders, no fees. I said yes.
